title: Jerusalem the Foundling and the Unfaithful Wife
summary: In the longest allegory in the book, God tells Jerusalem's history as the story of an abandoned newborn girl whom he rescued, raised, married, and adorned as a queen. She then turned her beauty and his gifts to other lovers, meaning idols and foreign powers, and even sacrificed her children. God announces that those same lovers will strip and destroy her, compares her unfavorably with her sisters Samaria and Sodom, and ends by promising to remember his covenant, establish an everlasting covenant, and make atonement for all she has done.
story: Chapter 16 is the second of three pictures of Jerusalem in chapters 15 to 17, and it is by far the most extended. Chapter 15 said the vine was worthless without fruit; chapter 16 retells the city's entire history to show that everything she had was a gift, and that she betrayed the giver. It is a history of grace answered by ingratitude. The chapter's ending matters as much as its middle: after the judgment comes a promise of an everlasting covenant and atonement (verses 60 to 63), one of the book's clearest statements of hope before the fall of Jerusalem. Ezekiel returns to the same metaphor, in even harsher form, in chapter 23, with two sisters representing Samaria and Jerusalem.
historical:
The chapter compresses centuries into a single life. Jerusalem was a Canaanite city, held by the Jebusites, until David captured it and made it his capital around 1000 BC (2 Samuel 5:6-9). That is why God says her father was an Amorite and her mother a Hittite (verse 3): Amorites and Hittites were names for the older peoples of the land, and the point is that Jerusalem had no noble pedigree. Her rise to be queen (verse 13) recalls the splendor of the kingdom under David and Solomon.

The lovers named in verses 26 to 29 are the great powers with whom Judah's kings made alliances instead of trusting God: Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon (Chaldea). King Ahaz, for example, sent temple silver and gold to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III for protection around 734 to 732 BC (2 Kings 16:7-9), and King Hezekiah welcomed envoys from Babylon and showed them his treasures (2 Kings 20:12-19). The daughters of the Philistines in verse 27 may recall the loss of Judah's territory; Sennacherib's own annals claim that after his invasion of Judah in 701 BC he gave captured Judean towns to Philistine kings. The sacrifice of children (verses 20 and 21) refers to a practice that 2 Kings and Jeremiah associate with the Valley of Ben-hinnom and the god Molech, which King Josiah tried to stamp out (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, had fallen to Assyria in 722 BC.
cultural:
Every detail of the opening scene was clear to an ancient reader. Newborns were washed, rubbed with salt (a practice believed to strengthen and cleanse the skin), and wrapped in cloths. An infant who received none of this and was left in an open field had been abandoned to die, a practice known in the ancient world, especially for unwanted girls. The rescuer's word, “Live,” is the whole of her future. When God later spreads his cloak over the grown young woman (verse 8), he uses a gesture of marriage and protection, the same one Ruth asked of Boaz (Ruth 3:9). The washing, anointing, fine clothes, and jewelry that follow were the gifts of a wealthy bridegroom to a bride.

The prophets often described the covenant between God and Israel as a marriage, and idolatry as adultery (Hosea 1 to 3; Jeremiah 2 and 3). The metaphor fit an ancient culture in which a marriage was an exclusive covenant and a wife's unfaithfulness was treated as a grave crime. The Law of Moses prescribed death for adultery (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22), and public stripping appears elsewhere as a punishment of shame (Hosea 2:3, 10). Ezekiel draws on these norms to describe what the city's lovers, the nations, will do when they turn on her. The punishment of verses 37 to 41 corresponds closely to what happens to a city under siege: its walls and shrines torn down, its wealth taken, its houses burned, its people killed. In the ancient Near East, cities were commonly personified as women, often as the wife or daughter of their god, which made the image natural for Ezekiel's first hearers.
literary: The chapter is an extended allegory in three movements. The first (verses 1 to 43) tells the story of the foundling who became a queen and then a prostitute, and announces her judgment. The second (verses 44 to 58) turns to a family proverb, “Like mother, like daughter,” and compares Jerusalem with her sisters Samaria and Sodom, finding her worse than both. The third (verses 59 to 63) promises a restored covenant. The key verb is “remember”: Jerusalem did not remember the days of her youth (verses 22 and 43), but God will remember his covenant made in those days (verse 60), and then Jerusalem will remember and be ashamed (verses 61 and 63). The language is deliberately shocking, crude by the standards of Scripture itself, and it was meant to shock the male elders and leaders who were Ezekiel's first audience by casting them as a disgraced wife.

outline.t: The abandoned newborn: God says Live
Beauty and gifts given to idols, and children sacrificed
Shrines in every street and alliances with the nations
Like mother, like daughter: Samaria and Sodom
Restoration of the sisters and Jerusalem's shame

doctrines.note: The chapter pictures the covenant as a marriage initiated entirely by God's grace. Jerusalem broke it, but God promises to remember it and establish an everlasting covenant (verse 60). The covenant's future rests on God's faithfulness, not Israel's.

Idolatry here takes religious and political forms: shrines and images, but also alliances with Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon. Both amount to trusting someone other than God with what only he can give. Its worst fruit is the sacrifice of children.

The chapter ends with God making atonement for all Jerusalem has done (verse 63). The Hebrew verb is the one used for the sacrifices of the Day of Atonement. God himself provides the covering for the sin the chapter has described so graphically.

Verse 49 names the sin of Sodom as arrogance, excess, complacency, and failure to help the poor and needy, alongside the abominations of verse 50. Ezekiel shows that sin includes indifference as well as open rebellion, and that the privileged are judged by what they did with their privilege.

words.note: Zanah, to be sexually unfaithful or to act as a prostitute. With its related noun it appears more than twenty times in this chapter. In the prophets it is the standard image for idolatry and faithless political alliances. The word is harsh because the betrayal it describes is serious, not because women are the particular object of blame; the image applies to the whole people, men first of all.

Berit, covenant, a binding agreement that creates a relationship with obligations on both sides. In this chapter the covenant is pictured as a marriage (verse 8). Jerusalem despised the oath by breaking it (verse 59), but God promises an everlasting covenant (verse 60), a phrase that looks toward the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31.

Zakhar, to remember. In Hebrew, remembering is more than recalling information; it means acting on what is remembered. Jerusalem's failure to remember her origins led to pride. God's remembering his covenant leads to restoration.

Kipper, to atone, cover, or make reconciliation. It is the key verb of Israel's sacrificial system, especially the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). In verse 63 God is the subject: he makes atonement, a striking promise at the end of a chapter of judgment.

christ: The marriage between God and his people, broken in this chapter, is restored in the New Testament through Christ. Paul describes Christ as a husband who loved the church and gave himself up for her to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word (Ephesians 5:25-27), language that echoes the washing and adorning of Ezekiel 16:9-14. Revelation ends with the bride of the Lamb clothed in fine linen (Revelation 19:7-8; 21:2). The New Testament also presents Jesus as the one through whom God makes atonement and establishes the new and everlasting covenant (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 13:20). In Ezekiel the bridegroom's love is betrayed and the unfaithful bride is judged; in the gospel the bridegroom bears the cost of the betrayal himself.

hard.q: How should we read a chapter that pictures God as a husband who exposes and punishes an unfaithful wife, especially for readers who have suffered abuse?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real and should be named plainly. The chapter uses sexually explicit language and describes a woman stripped, stoned, and cut to pieces by a mob, with the husband's jealousy as the reason. Many readers, including many women and survivors of abuse, find that the imagery echoes the words and patterns of abusive relationships, and the text has sometimes been misused to justify controlling or violent men. Interpreters respond in several ways. Some stress that this is a metaphor for a city, addressed to a mostly male leadership, and that the punishment describes the historical sack of Jerusalem by the nations she trusted, not a model for any marriage. Others add that the chapter's frame is grace: it begins with rescue and ends with atonement, so the husband's aim is restoration, not destruction. Feminist and trauma-informed interpreters argue that even as metaphor the imagery carries a cost, because it draws on and can reinforce ancient norms that treated women's bodies as the site of shame, and they call for reading it with open eyes, lament, and resistance to its misuse. These views are not mutually exclusive, and many careful readers hold parts of each.

What can be said without qualification is that nothing in this chapter permits any person to abuse a spouse. The New Testament calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). If you are being hurt or threatened by a partner, that is not God's will for you, and help is available. In the United States you can call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233; elsewhere, contact local emergency services or a domestic violence service, and consider speaking with a trusted pastor or counselor.

questions: The chapter begins with a helpless newborn whom God tells to live. What does it mean for your view of yourself that everything good you have began as a gift?
Ezekiel names Sodom's sin as arrogance, excess, complacency, and neglect of the poor. Which of these is most present in your community, or in you?
How do you hold together the severity of this chapter and its closing promise of atonement? What does each tell you about God?
